title: Spring's longing
hook: in the spring months the bride hears the koel and longs for the Beloved (Tukhari Barah Maha)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanak's twelve months: a poem that opens with listen, and a bride who can't live a moment without her Beloved. Today the year begins.

A bird calls from a mango tree, early, before the house is awake. Then again, a little farther off. The poem names it: the koel, singing in the mango tree. Guru Nanak puts it right at the start of his year. The month is Chet, spring, and everything is beautiful. That's the trouble. When the whole world is in bloom, the one thing missing is easier to hear.
screen: `A BIRD IN THE MANGO TREE.` → `CHET: EVERYTHING IN BLOOM.` → `THE MISSING ONE IS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Here's Chet, in plain English, not word for word. Chet is good, spring is lovely, the bumblebees are beautiful, the forest is in flower. Then the koel sings sweetly in the mango tree, and the bride asks: how can I bear this pain inside me? The bumblebee circles the flowering branch, and she says, how can I live, mother? I'm dying. Notice: the poem doesn't call spring bad. It calls it lovely. But when the one you love is far away, beauty can hurt more than gray skies. Every lovely thing points at who isn't there to see it. Then Vaisakh, and the trees join in: Vaisakh is good, and the branches put on new clothes, fresh leaves like an outfit for a wedding. And the bride stands looking at the door. Come home, Beloved, have mercy. Carry me across this hard ocean. Without You, I'm not worth half a shell. In Sikh reading, the bride is the soul and the Beloved is God. So spring is the moment life is fullest around you, and something in you still says: not yet, not without You. The poem doesn't shush that. It treats the ache as part of love, the sign she hasn't forgotten who she's waiting for. That's today's line: the bird calls.
screen: `CHET: THE KOEL IN THE MANGO TREE.` · `BEAUTY CAN MAKE MISSING LOUDER.` · `VAISAKH: BRANCHES IN NEW CLOTHES.` · `THE BRIDE WATCHES THE DOOR.` · then, large: `THE BIRD CALLS.`

segments.voice: Open a window or step outside if you can, or just listen to the room, and wait for a bird, any bird, near or far. If one calls, follow the sound until it fades; if none comes, notice the waiting itself, the leaning-in, the small hope, the bride at the door. If you pray, say Waheguru softly between the calls.
Spring's longing. In Guru Nanak's Chet and Vaisakh, the koel sings and the trees put on new clothes, and all that beauty makes the absent Beloved felt more. Today's word.
Your line: the bird calls. Spring is lovely, and still the bride watches the door. That's day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's longing in each month as the soul's longing for God.

chat.says: Why would Nanak's poem about spring sound so sad?
options: Because all that beauty makes the missing Beloved felt more; the ache is part of love.
Because spring was a hard, hungry season for the farmers of old Punjab.
Because the bride has given up on her Beloved ever coming home.
chat.meaning: Nanak's Chet calls spring lovely; beauty makes the absent Beloved felt more, and the ache is the sign the bride hasn't forgotten.

koel.meaning: a songbird that calls from the mango tree in Chet

Chet.meaning: the spring month that opens the poem's year

Vaisakh.meaning: the spring month when branches put on new clothes

Waheguru.meaning: the Sikh word of wonder for God
